# The Signal at Asterion

Before sunrise, Mara crossed the empty observatory and listened to the old ventilation fans count out the seconds. The lights along the eastern rail woke one by one, cold blue at first, then warm enough to soften the steel. Beneath the cracked dome, the Asterion array waited in perfect silence.

At four seventeen in the morning, the array found a pulse where no pulse belonged. It was faint, deliberate, and patient. Now it had returned in groups of three, leaving just enough quiet between them for wonder to become fear. Mara held one hand above the receiver while Wren, a broad-shouldered man in a rain-dark coat, stood between her and the exit.

<!-- yakbox:speech:speaker name=wren -->

“Mara, step away from the console,” Wren said. “If that signal recognizes you, we may never get another chance to leave this room.”

<!-- yakbox:speech:speaker name=mara -->

“I have spent twelve years wondering why it called my name,” Mara said. “I will not let fear answer for me again.”

The receiver clicked beneath her fingertips. Across the observatory, dormant screens filled with the same pale waveform, each pulse a little stronger than the last. Wren moved closer, but he kept his hands where Mara could see them.

<!-- yakbox:speech:speaker name=wren -->

“You think this is an invitation,” Wren said. “It is learning how long you hesitate, how quickly you breathe, and which words will keep you listening.”

<!-- yakbox:speech:speaker name=mara -->

“Then let it learn this,” Mara replied. “I am still here, and this time I decide when the conversation ends.”

Wren looked toward the emergency cutoff. For one suspended second, neither of them moved. Rain ticked against the dome, the ventilation fans turned, and the signal gathered itself into a thin, impossible chord.

<!-- yakbox:speech:speaker name=wren -->

“If you answer, I cannot protect you from what comes next,” Wren said, his voice low now, almost lost beneath the rising tone.

<!-- yakbox:speech:speaker name=mara -->

“I am not asking you to protect me,” Mara said. “I am asking you to trust me long enough to hear the truth.”

<!-- yakbox:speech:pause ms=450 -->

The final tone arrived. Mara drew a careful breath, and the room seemed to draw one with her. Then a voice, distant but unmistakably human, said her name.
